rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)|; vertical lines: use inclinations α
tan θ(full) = 4/3 ⟹ θ ≈ 53.13° = 2 × 26.57°

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: NEB-style practice beyond the verified PYQs recorded on the parent canonicals.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Slopes fail on verticals; inclinations never do.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The fraction verdict*** - tan = 2 > 1 certifies obtuse without any degree conversion - the comparison with 1 is the whole test.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: The axis-angle reading is the universal fallback: every line has an inclination, vertical or not.  ·  tan theta = |(m2-m1)/(1+m1 m2)| for finite slopes; vertical lines use axis angles (inclination difference). Threshold: tan < 1 acute, > 1 obtuse - always a fraction comparison. Here: horizontal bisector vs L1 gives tan = 2 > 1 (obtuse); vertical bisector vs L2 gives 26.57 degrees < 45 (acute). Doubling closure: full angle tan = 4/3, twice the half-angle matches.…

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The tan θ Verification II (Axis-Parallel Bisectors) This canonical runs the **tangent verification on the second worked pair** — the lines 2x + y − 7 = 0 and 2x − y + 1 = 0 with bisectors 2x − 3 = 0 (acute) and y = 4 (obtuse). The vertical bisector exercises the axis-angle fallback where slopes fail, completing the verification toolkit.  ·  ## 2. Theorem Mirror (as used here) - **Angle between two lines:** tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)| — valid for finite slopes. - **Axis-angle fallback:** a line's inclination α = atan(m) (or 90° for vertical); the angle between two lines is the difference of inclinations, taken acutely. - **The threshold test:** tan θ < 1 ⟹ the candidate bisects the acute angle; tan θ > 1 ⟹ the obtuse one.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Vertical bisector? Compare inclinations with the x-axis - the angle difference is the answer.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB-style (6m): Using the tangent formula, verify that y = 4 is the obtuse angle bisector of the lines 2x + y − 7 = 0 and 2x − y + 1 = 0.** — **Slopes:** bisector y = 4 ⟹ m_b = 0; L₁: y = 7 − 2x ⟹ m₁ = −2. **Tangent:** tan θ = |(0 − (−2))/(1 + (0)(−2))| = **2**.…  ·  **NEB-style (6m): Using axis angles (the vertical-line fallback), verify that 2x − 3 = 0 is the acute angle bisector of 2x + y − 7 = 0 and 2x − y + 1 = 0.** — **Inclinations:** L₂ (2x − y + 1 = 0 ⟹ y = 2x + 1) has α₂ = atan 2 ≈ 63.43°; the vertical bisector has α_b = 90°. **Angle between:** |90° − 63.43°| = **26.57°**.…

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Close with the doubling check: full angle = 2 x half-angle, computed independently.

rows.label: Classified table
rows.text: Bisector checks — three verification instruments, classified · Instrument | What it tests | Verdict it gives · tan(theta/2) equality | Angle from bisector to line 1 vs line 2 | Equal => genuine bisector · Distance equality | Perpendicular distance of a test point to each line | Equal => point truly on a bisector · Slope product | Product of the two bisectors' slopes | -1 => the two bisectors are perpendicular (always true)

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The acute and obtuse half-angle tangents are reciprocals - complementary angles in the arithmetic.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (5m): Compute the full angle between 2x + y − 7 = 0 and 2x − y + 1 = 0, and verify the doubling closure against the verified half-angle.** — **Full angle:** tan θ = |(2 − (−2))/(1 + (−2)(2))| = 4/|−3| = **4/3** ⟹ θ ≈ 53.13° (acute angle between the lines).…  ·  **NEB-style (6m): The half-angle tangents for this pair are 1/2 (acute side) and 2 (obtuse side). Explain their reciprocal relationship and verify it via the complementary-angle identity.** — **The relationship:** the acute half-angle (26.57°) and the obtuse half-angle (63.43°) are complementary…

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 3. Deep Conceptual — Where Slopes Fail, Angles Take Over - The vertical bisector 2x − 3 = 0 has **no slope** — the tangent formula cannot even be written for it. The axis-angle reading (a line's direction is its inclination α; the angle between lines is |α₂ − α₁| taken acutely) is the universal fallback, and it handles vertical lines as naturally as any other.…  ·  ## 4. Deep Conceptual — Threshold Comparisons as Fraction Arithmetic - Every verdict in this canonical is a **comparison with 1**, never an angle computation: tan = 2 > 1 (obtuse), tan = 1/2 < 1 (acute). Keeping the arithmetic in fractions preserves exactness and speed; converting to decimals or degrees too early invites rounding doubt.…  ·  ## 5. Worked Example Types - **Type A — horizontal bisector audit:** plain slope tangent, threshold comparison. - **Type B — vertical bisector audit:** axis-angle fallback, same threshold. - **Type C — doubling closure:** full angle = 2 × half-angle, all in fractions. - **Type D — reciprocal signature:** the two half-angle tangents multiply to 1.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Verify via tangent that y = 4 is the obtuse bisector of 2x + y − 7 = 0 and 2x − y + 1 = 0.  ·  Verify via axis angles that 2x − 3 = 0 is the acute bisector of the same pair.  ·  Compute the full angle between the two lines and check it equals twice the half-angle.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ## 6.
